Comparisons with as…as / Not as… as and Negative Comparative Forms

When we want to say that two things are or are not equal we use the structure not + as + adjective + as.

By using less and an adjective, we establish that the first thing being compared does not share the same characteristics as the second one.

This structure is normally used to establish a comparison between two things that share the same characteristics:

  • An IT procurement is as complex as any other contract.


    • If we use this structure with a negative verb, we establish that the first thing mentioned is “less” than the second thing. The same meaning can be obtained by using less and an adjective:

  • Signing a contract for a licensed software isn't as simple as many people think.
  • Signing a contract for a licensed software is less simple than many people think.
It is not as straightforward as buying a property or selling a business.
It is not as simple as I thought.
It's less practical to have just a very few suppliers.
Imperatives to Talk about Tips
Imperative sentences are used to either give commands or to give friendly informal advice.

The imperative form of a verb is its base form. Imperative sentences are usually short and simple, but they can also be long and complex sentences that convey a lot of information.

In imperative sentences the information is direct and the use of a subject is not necessary as it is implied that the subject is “you”:

  • Try to read everything carefully before signing the contract.

    • To make a negative imperative place “do not” or “don't” before the verb:

  • Do not sign without reading.
Try to include your own terms and conditions in your RFP or, if it isn't possible, arrange an acceptable position in the supplier's contract.
Also, check if you're eligible to use the Government Information Technology Contracting (GITC) framework when acquiring the IT Service.
Do not downselect before the contract is negotiated.
Try not to let the suppliers know they have been selected until the terms have been agreed, and try to keep final negotiations with a least three potential suppliers.

images.text:
Consultant: So, now let's move on to clarifying some doubts you may have regarding the IT procurement contract.
Client: Isn't that just another informal transaction?
Consultant: Not really. It is not as straightforward as buying a property or selling a business. The IT that is procured is often critical for a company's day to day operations, and as such, it deserves some management and legal attention. Some people don't even read the contract before signing it.
Client: I think I do that sometimes.

Consultant: Well, you shouldn't. By simply signing, the solution deliverables and associated timeframes may not be very clear and you might not be able to sue the supplier if the solution doesn't work or its performance isn't as good as expected.
Client: It is not as simple as I thought.
Consultant: Try to include your own terms and conditions in your RFP or, if it isn't possible, arrange an acceptable position in the supplier's contract. Also, check if you're eligible to use the Government Information Technology Contracting (GITC) framework when acquiring the IT Service.

Client: Wow, that's quite a lot to take into account. Now, what If I have many potential suppliers?
Consultant: Do not downselect before the contract is negotiated. Try not to let the suppliers know they have been selected until the terms have been agreed, and try to keep final negotiations with a least three potential suppliers. It's less practical to have just a very few suppliers, once they know they have the job they're usually difficult to negotiate with.
Client: Understood! Any further recommendation?
Consultant: I have to insist on checking the contract before signing it. You couldend up accepting an "all care and no responsibility” kind of agreement. Make sure you're not sued for infringing a third party's intellectual property rights.
